title: The trees that live for others
hookLine: midday heat, cowherd boys resting in the shade, and Krishna starts praising the trees
carry: life, wealth, mind and words: all can be seva

cards: Midday, far out in the forest, and the sun is fierce. Krishna and the cowherd boys have taken the cows a long way from the village, and the boys are hot and worn out. They duck under the trees for shade.
A rest stop, nothing more. And Krishna looks up into the branches and starts talking about the trees, the way you'd talk about a person you admire.
It's a short scene in the Bhagavata's tenth book, in the middle of a summer day, and it holds a whole picture of service.

teach.b: Look at these blessed trees, he says, in paraphrase. They live entirely for others. They bear wind and rain, heat and frost themselves, and they shelter us from all of it.

teach.h: LEAF, FRUIT, SHADE, BARK, EVEN ASH.
teach.b: Then he lists what a tree gives: its leaves, flowers and fruit, its shade, its roots, bark and wood, its fragrance and sap, even its ashes, even its young shoots. No one who comes to a tree goes away with nothing.
Then the verse that turns the scene into a teaching.

This much, he says, is the fruit of being born: to keep doing good for others with your life, your wealth, your understanding and your words. Notice the four. In Sanskrit they're breath, wealth, understanding and speech.
That's the Bhagavata's own map of seva, and it's built for a vocation, because everyone has at least one. Some days the seva is money. Some days it's what you know.
Some days it's your hours and your hands. And some days it's only a word, but a word is on the list. The tree doesn't pick one gift and refuse the rest.
It gives whatever part of it is asked for. And notice who's listening. Not sages.
Boys who look after cows. Krishna doesn't take them to a temple to learn about service.

teach.h: A LESSON IN THE SHADE YOU SIT IN.
teach.b: He points at the shade they're already sitting in.

how: Hindu teachers point to Krishna's praise of the trees in the Bhagavata's tenth book as a picture of service, and its closing verse, on doing good with life, wealth, understanding and words, is recited in talks on seva.

o: service as life's work, like a tree that gives
a calling to plant and care for forests
giving only money to those in need

games.q: the trees and the four gifts — tap the pairs.
p: rest in the shade, far from home
how a life does good for others

s: Krishna gives this teaching to sages in a temple
he gives it to cowherd boys resting under trees in the midday heat.
Krishna says no one who comes to a tree goes away with nothing
leaves, fruit, shade, bark, wood, even ash: something is always given.
in the verse, doing good only counts if it costs money
life, wealth, understanding and words are all on the list.

games.q: the temple is collecting for the festival kitchen and Priya has six dollars. by Krishna's verse under the trees, what can she give?
o: nothing worth counting until she has real money.
her hours, what she knows, a kind word, or the six dollars.
only prayers; giving is for adults with wealth.
games.why: Krishna says the fruit of a birth is doing good with life, wealth, understanding and words. like a tree, you give whatever part is asked for.

practice: Let Krishna's four gifts come one at a time: life, where your time could help someone; wealth, something small to give; understanding, something you know that someone needs; words, who could use a kind one.
Don't plan it all; let one of the four light up and rest there, offering it to the One you pray to, if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Seva as vocation. Service as a life's work: like the tree, giving with life, wealth, understanding and words.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tree; in this scene, Krishna's picture of a life lived for others.

carryVoice: Your line: life, wealth, mind and words: all can be seva. Even a kind word counts as giving. Go gently.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.22.30–31 (far from the village in the heat, the boys shelter under the trees)
